1324.title: The serpent who teaches the seat
1324.hook: the serpent who holds up Vishnu comes down as a teacher, and starts with how to sit
1324.carry: posture and breath are rungs toward a still mind
1324.tomorrow: who taught yoga first, and who overheard?
1324.howItsDone: In yoga traditions that follow Patanjali, posture and breath come after ethical restraints and observances and lead toward concentration and meditation; some classes open with an invocation to Patanjali, pictured as the serpent Adishesha.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breath again: a student asked too much, and the teacher drew breath as a king sending officers out to the villages.
screen: `THE BREATH AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Out on the cosmic ocean, Vishnu rests on a great serpent with a thousand heads. Its name is Shesha, also called Ananta, the endless. It holds him steady, coiled and at ease, through the long night between worlds. Tradition tells that this serpent once came down to teach. A woman named Gonika stood praying with her palms cupped, and a tiny snake dropped into them. He grew up to be Patanjali, the teacher of the Yoga Sutras; tradition hears his name as fallen, pata, into folded palms, anjali. Today: what he teaches about sitting, breathing, and what both are for.
screen: `VISHNU'S SERPENT SEAT.` → `A SNAKE IN CUPPED HANDS.` → `PATANJALI, TEACHER OF THE SEAT.`

segments.voice: That's a legend from later tradition; the Sutras never tell his life. But notice what it makes of him: the serpent who is God's own couch becomes the teacher of the seat. Patanjali opens with yoga's aim, in paraphrase: yoga is the stilling of the movements of the mind, and then the seer rests in its own nature. That's the big teaching. In Hindu yoga the goal isn't a body. It's a mind quiet enough for the self, the seer, to be seen. To get there he lays out eight limbs, ashtanga. First, how you treat others and yourself. Then posture, then breath, and on up to meditation and absorption. Posture and breath are rungs three and four. Now the seat. Patanjali asks for one that is steady and easy, sthira and sukha. It comes, he says, as effort loosens and the mind rests on the endless, ananta. Some teachers hear the serpent's own name in that word: sit the way Ananta holds Vishnu, firm and at ease. That's a reading, not the text. Only after the seat comes pranayama, which he defines as a pause in the flow of breathing in and breathing out. Not a push. Its fruit: the mind becomes fit for concentration. Some yoga classes open with a chant bowing to Patanjali as that white, thousand-headed serpent. They're borrowing a ladder whose top is the self. So when a class feels like a workout, remember: the stretch is a low rung, and the climb is toward a quiet mind. If you have heart or lung trouble, or get dizzy, keep breath practice gentle and ask a doctor first.
screen: `YOGA: A STILL MIND` · `POSTURE AND BREATH: RUNGS 3 AND 4` · `A STEADY, EASY SEAT; THEN A PAUSE` · `THE STRETCH IS A LOW RUNG`

segments.voice: Sit the way the serpent holds Vishnu: steady first, then easy, shoulders down, jaw loose, effort loosening a little with each breath out. Only then turn to the breath, and don't steer it; if a natural little pause comes after a breath out, notice it without stretching it, and if anything strains, go back to the seat. If you pray, you can let the stillness be your prayer.
The breath again. In Patanjali, a steady, easy seat comes first, and pranayama is a pause in the flow of breath, both rungs toward a still mind. Today's word.

1325.title: Shiva's lesson, heard from inside a fish
1325.hook: Shiva teaches yoga to Parvati by the sea, a boy inside a fish listens in, and a line of teachers begins
1325.carry: yoga passes from guru to student, back to shiva
1325.tomorrow: can a single breath be a gift?
1325.howItsDone: In hatha yoga lineages, breath practices are learned gradually from a teacher; the Hatha Yoga Pradipika opens by bowing to Shiva as the first teacher, and many Hindus honor their teachers on Guru Purnima.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breath again: the serpent who holds up Vishnu came down as Patanjali, and taught that posture and breath are rungs toward a still mind.
screen: `THE BREATH AGAIN.`

segments.voice: On a lonely shore, the story goes, Shiva sat with Parvati and taught her the secret of yoga. But someone else was listening. Down in the water, a great fish had swallowed a boy, and from inside it he took in every word. Shiva noticed, and blessed the listener, and the boy came out a master. He's remembered as Matsyendranath, lord of the fish. His student was Gorakhnath, and from the two of them comes a whole line of yogis. Today: the line of teachers hatha yoga is handed down through, and why its own manual tells you to go slowly.
screen: `SHIVA TEACHES BY THE SEA.` → `A BOY IN A FISH OVERHEARS.` → `A LINE OF TEACHERS BEGINS.`

segments.voice: That's a legend of the Nath yogis, and tellings differ; in some, the fish itself is the listener. The claim is the point: for the Naths and the hatha yogis, yoga isn't invented; it's received. It comes down from Shiva, the first teacher, one student at a time. That's guru parampara, the line of teachers, and it's one of Hinduism's deepest habits: knowledge that matters is passed hand to hand, from a guru to a student who is ready. Hindus even keep a day for it, Guru Purnima, a full moon when students honor their teachers. The Hatha Yoga Pradipika shows the habit. Its author, Svatmarama, opens by bowing to Adinatha, the first lord, a name for Shiva, who taught hatha yoga as a stairway for anyone wanting to climb to the higher yoga of the still mind. Then he names the line: Matsyendra, Gorakhnath and others. The body practice is a stair, not the summit. And what's handed down is handed down carefully. In paraphrase: as a lion, an elephant or a tiger is tamed little by little, so the breath; otherwise it harms the one who practices. It lists what careless practice brings, cough and pain among them, and also promises that right practice ends every disease; no doctor would promise that, so leave that line on the page. Keep the guru and the slowness. That's why, in traditional yoga, you don't learn breath practice from a stranger's video. You learn it from a teacher, who learned it from one, back toward Shiva by the sea.
screen: `GURU PARAMPARA: THE LINE OF TEACHERS` · `HATHA, A STAIR TO THE STILL MIND` · `TAMED LITTLE BY LITTLE` · `KEEP THE GURU, LEAVE THE CURE-ALL`

segments.voice: Let the breath move on its own and watch its pace, the way a keeper watches a lion before ever reaching out a hand; if anything strains, back to ordinary breathing. Then bring to mind one teacher who handed you something that mattered, and whoever taught them, and let one breath of thanks go back down that line. If you pray, you can bow inwardly to the guru, as many Hindus do before practice.
The breath again. In the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, breath is tamed little by little, like a lion, and learned in a line of teachers that begins with Shiva. Today's word.

1326.title: Breath poured as an offering
1326.hook: in the Gita's list of offerings, some people offer their breath, and it sits in a row with everyone else's gift
1326.carry: even a breath can be yajna, an offering
1326.tomorrow: breath is Brahman, so why keep looking?
1326.howItsDone: Many Hindus chant Gita 4.24 ('the offering is Brahman…') before meals, and some treat daily actions, breathing among them, as offerings in the spirit of the Gita's fourth chapter.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breath again: by the sea a fish overheard Shiva teaching yoga, and the breath has been handed down, teacher to student, ever since.
screen: `THE BREATH AGAIN.`

segments.voice: What would it mean to give a breath away? Not to hold it, or push it, or count it. To offer it, the way a person sets a flower down in front of an image or pours a spoon of ghee into a fire. In the fourth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna walks Arjuna through a long list of offerings people make. Wealth, study, discipline, the restraint of the senses. And in the middle of the list, quietly, breath. Today: what the Gita does with the breath, and the verse that turns a family dinner into an offering.
screen: `GIVE A BREATH AWAY?` → `A LIST OF OFFERINGS.` → `BREATH, IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. Some, Krishna says, offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath, holding the path of both, given over to the practice of breath. The breath going in is poured into the breath going out, like ghee into a fire, and back again. Breathing itself becomes a yajna, a sacrifice. That's the teaching: in the Gita, any act can be an offering, not only what's poured into a temple fire. Look at the company breath keeps. Some offer their senses into the fire of restraint. Some offer their possessions. Some offer austerity, some study, some yoga. And a short line sums up the row: all of these know what sacrifice is. You'll sometimes hear that the Gita crowns breath control as the highest yoga. It doesn't. Breath gets its own careful verse, in a row of gifts. The point isn't what you get from the breath, but what you give with it. A few verses earlier sits the line that makes this a daily habit. In paraphrase: the offering is Brahman, the ghee is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman. Many Hindus chant that verse before eating, so the plate becomes an offering and the meal a small yajna. In the fifth chapter, the Gita mentions evening out the in-breath and out-breath within the nostrils, and there too breath serves a larger aim: a person free of desire, fear and anger. Eating, breathing, the most ordinary things, can be given.
screen: `IN-BREATH POURED INTO OUT-BREATH` · `YAJNA: ANY ACT CAN BE AN OFFERING` · `THE VERSE CHANTED BEFORE MEALS` · `NOT WHAT YOU GET, BUT WHAT YOU GIVE`

segments.voice: Notice the breath in arriving and let it flow into the breath out without a seam, then the breath out turning into the breath in, like the gentlest offering: something set down, not thrown. If you pray, you can offer your breathing, just as it is, to God, as some Hindus do; if you don't, you can simply let it go with thanks.
The breath again. In the Gita, some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, one gift in a row of many. Today's word.

1327.title: Bhrigu's second answer
1327.hook: a son keeps bringing his father an answer, and the father keeps sending him back, past food, past breath
1327.carry: the self lies deeper than body and breath
1327.tomorrow: who rose out of the furrow?
1327.howItsDone: The Taittiriya Upanishad's story of Bhrigu is studied in Vedanta as a teaching on the layers of a person, food, breath, mind, understanding and bliss, and is also chanted in Vedic recitation.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breath again: in the Gita, some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and many Hindus offer their meals the same way.
screen: `THE BREATH AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Breath is Brahman. That's the second answer a young man named Bhrigu brings home to his father, Varuna, in the third part of the Taittiriya Upanishad. This path met him over food, his first answer. The clue hasn't changed: Brahman is that from which beings are born, by which they live, and into which they return. Go and practice, and find out. Food fit the clue, and still he was sent out again. Now he's back with breath. On the last day of a season of breath: the step after food, what the Upanishad says breath is, and why the son still isn't done.
screen: `BREATH IS BRAHMAN.` → `THE SECOND ANSWER.` → `ONE HONEST ANSWER AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's how the second answer comes, in paraphrase. Bhrigu practices again, and comes to see that breath is Brahman. From breath beings are born, by breath they live, into breath they return. It fits the clue. The second part of the same Upanishad has a short verse that says why: the gods breathe along with breath, and so do people, and so do animals. Breath is the life of beings, so it's called the life of all. While there's life, there's breath. And still Varuna says, practice again. Bhrigu goes on, to mind, to understanding, and at last to bliss, and this time he isn't sent away. The same Upanishad gives the map behind his steps, and Vedanta teachers make much of it. A person is like a set of sheaths, koshas, one inside the next. A self made of food: the body. Inside it, a self made of breath. Inside that, mind; then understanding; and innermost, bliss. That's the teaching: you are more than your body, and more than your breath. Many Vedanta teachers read it this way: the true self, atman, is what every layer rests on, deeper than all of them. Breath, in this tradition, is offered, tamed, watched, called the life of all. It's a doorway, not the house. On a day when you're out of breath, the breath is a good place to start, and Varuna would say: keep going in.
screen: `BREATH IS BRAHMAN` · `BREATH IS THE LIFE OF BEINGS` · `FIVE SHEATHS: FOOD, BREATH, MIND, UNDERSTANDING, BLISS` · `THE SELF LIES DEEPER`

segments.voice: Climb Bhrigu's steps slowly: notice the body, the food that built it, the weight on the seat; then the breath, coming and going on its own; then the mind, thoughts arriving and leaving; then the knowing that is aware of all of it. Then simply rest, and let whatever ease is there be enough. If you pray, you can rest in God's presence.

segments.voice: A king is plowing. Not a farmer, a king, walking behind the plow, clearing a field. And out of the furrow, out of the turned earth, a girl rises. He lifts her up, takes her home, and raises her as his own daughter. The king is Janaka of Mithila. The girl is Sita. A new season starts today: the women of the epics, heard in their own words where the texts give them words. It starts with the one who came out of the ground.
screen: `A KING BEHIND THE PLOW.` → `A GIRL RISES FROM THE FURROW.` → `A SEASON OF THE EPICS' WOMEN.`

segments.voice: The story comes late in the first book of Valmiki's Ramayana, from Janaka's own mouth. In paraphrase: while I was plowing the field, a girl rose from the earth. I found her while clearing the ground, and she is known by the name Sita. She was not born from a womb, he adds, and he calls her his daughter. Then he sets a test for her suitors: string the great bow of Shiva. In the next chapter, Rama lifts it, and it breaks. Three things to hold as this season begins. First, the name. Tradition hears in it the Sanskrit word for a furrow, the line the plow cuts. Second, her father. The Upanishads tell of a King Janaka who loved to ask about the self, the one heard earlier on this path questioning Yajnavalkya, and tradition links Sita's father to that king or his line. Third, the shape of her story. She comes out of the earth at the start, and in the Ramayana's last book the ground opens and takes her home. That's why Hindus call her Bhumija, born of the earth, and it rests on a teaching older than her story: the earth is a goddess and a mother, Bhudevi. Many Hindus still say a short prayer in the morning before their feet touch the floor, asking Mother Earth to forgive them for stepping on her. The season ahead follows Sita's own words and choices. It starts with the ground under everyone's feet.
screen: `JANAKA TELLS IT IN HIS OWN WORDS` · `A NAME THAT CARRIES THE FIELD` · `FROM THE EARTH, AND BACK TO IT` · `BHUDEVI: THE EARTH AS MOTHER`

segments.voice: Let your weight drop and notice exactly where the floor or the earth meets you, the feet, the seat, the hands, settling a little more with each breath out onto the same ground that was under Sita, turned, planted, walked on. If you pray, you can greet the earth as a mother, as many Hindus do before stepping down in the morning; otherwise, simply rest on it with thanks.
Sita. In Valmiki, Janaka finds her rising from the earth as he plows, and tradition hears the furrow in her name. Today's word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sita is earth's daughter, and the earth is mother: a girl rising out of the furrow as King Janaka plowed, the earth's own daughter.
screen: `SITA IS EARTH'S DAUGHTER, AND THE EARTH IS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: I will walk ahead of you. That, in paraphrase, is Sita's answer when Rama comes to tell her he's been sent into the forest, and that she should stay behind. The crown he was promised has been taken away. He's leaving soon. He has a careful speech ready about how she should live in Ayodhya while he's gone: honor his parents, don't praise him in front of the new heir. Sita doesn't take the speech. She takes the floor. Today: the argument in Valmiki's second book, where Sita's own words decide where she goes.
screen: `I WILL WALK AHEAD OF YOU.` → `A CAREFUL SPEECH, REFUSED.` → `SITA'S OWN WORDS DECIDE.`

segments.voice: She starts with a reason. A father, a mother, a brother, a son, she says, each lives by their own lot. A wife shares her husband's. If he is sent to the forest, so is she. Then she gets practical. I'll go first, and tread down the thorns and the sharp grass on the path. The forest with you is better to me than any palace without you. Rama tries again. He describes the forest honestly: wild animals, cold, hunger, sleeping on the ground. And here the text lets Sita get angry. In paraphrase: what was my father thinking, she asks, when he took you as a son-in-law? Did he think you were a man, when you're a woman in a man's form? It's a sharp line, and Valmiki keeps it. Then she weeps, and holds him, and Rama gives way. Come, he says. Her argument rests on a Hindu teaching about marriage. A wife is called sahadharmini: one who walks in dharma together with her husband. It's why, at a Hindu wedding, the couple take seven steps together before the sacred fire, and why many rites are done by the two side by side. Sita takes that teaching and turns it into an argument Rama can't refuse. Some readers hear devotion here first; others hear a woman choosing her own road against the man trying to choose it for her. The text holds both, and gives her the words either way. The thorns she promises to tread down are hers to tread.
screen: `A WIFE SHARES HER HUSBAND'S LOT` · `I'LL TREAD DOWN THE THORNS` · `SAHADHARMINI: ONE DHARMA, WALKED TOGETHER` · `DEVOTION, AND HER OWN ROAD`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one road ahead of you, a hard conversation, a move, a long week, and let someone you love come to mind alongside it. Ask quietly whether there's a thorn on that path you could tread down first, for them, and don't plan it; just breathe with whatever shows itself. If you pray, you can hold that person before God.

segments.voice: A single blade of grass. In Valmiki's fifth book, the Sundara Kanda, that's what Sita sets down between herself and Ravana. She's a captive in his city of Lanka, kept in a grove of ashoka trees, guarded day and night. He comes to her with jewels, promises and threats. She doesn't look at him. She picks up a blade of grass, places it between them, and speaks to the grass. Today: two choices Sita makes in the grove, both in her own words, and the second is a no to the one who has come to find her.
screen: `A SINGLE BLADE OF GRASS.` → `A CAPTIVE IN THE ASHOKA GROVE.` → `TWO CHOICES, IN HER OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: The first choice is the grass. Ravana offers her his kingdom, and his queens as her servants. Sita answers through the blade of grass, in paraphrase: turn your mind back to your own wives. I am not for you, the way the light belongs to the sun. Give me back to Rama, if you want to live. The grass is a wall made of almost nothing. It says: I won't even speak to you face to face. The second choice comes later. Hanuman, Rama's messenger, slips into the grove and shows her Rama's ring, so she knows he's real. Then he offers: climb on my back, and I'll carry you across the sea. Sita says no, and the text keeps her reasons. You might drop me over the water, or be attacked on the way. I won't willingly touch the body of any man but Rama. And this is Rama's to finish: let him come, defeat Ravana, and take me back himself. Then she gives Hanuman a jewel from her hair and a private memory from the forest, so Rama will know the message is truly hers. That's the teaching tradition draws from the grove: dharma isn't only for easy days. Sita holds hers as a captive, with nothing but a blade of grass and Rama in her mind, and she still sets the terms of her own rescue. It's one reason many Hindus read the Sundara Kanda in hard times: it's the book where a captive holds firm, and hope arrives.
screen: `SHE SPEAKS THROUGH A BLADE OF GRASS` · `THE RING, AND THE OFFER OF A RIDE` · `SITA SAYS NO, AND GIVES REASONS` · `DHARMA HELD, EVEN AS A CAPTIVE`

segments.voice: Sita in the grove kept Rama in mind, day after day. Sit, and with each breath out, silently say a name you trust; many Hindus use Ram. If something keeps pressing on you, let that name sit between you and it, quiet as her blade of grass, and notice you can still choose where your attention goes. If you don't pray, choose one word you'd want to stand on.
